## MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark

MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark was authored by Niklas Muennighoff, Nouamane Tazi, Loic Magne, and Nils Reimers, published at EACL 2023. The paper introduces the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), which spans 8 embedding tasks covering a total of 58 datasets and 112 languages. Through the benchmarking of 33 models on MTEB, the authors establish the most comprehensive benchmark of text embeddings to date.

The researchers find that no particular text embedding method dominates across all tasks, suggesting that the field has yet to converge on a universal text embedding method and scale it up sufficiently to provide state-of-the-art results on all embedding tasks.

**Paper Details:**

The paper was published at NeurIPS 2021 in the Datasets and Benchmarks Track. The authors are Nandan Thakur, Nils Reimers, Andreas Rücklé, Abhishek Srivastava, and Iryna Gurevych.

**Overview:**

The paper addresses how existing neural information retrieval (IR) models have often been studied in homogeneous and narrow settings, which has considerably limited insights into their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization capabilities. To address this, the authors introduce Benchmarking-IR (BEIR), a robust and heterogeneous evaluation benchmark for information retrieval, leveraging a careful selection of 18 publicly available datasets from diverse text retrieval tasks and domains, and evaluate 10 state-of-the-art retrieval systems including lexical, sparse, dense, late-interaction, and re-ranking architectures.

## Key Research Findings

Dense retrieval model performance is surprisingly sensitive to both random initialization and data shuffle, with models showing a very wide range of performance on BEIR benchmarks despite identical loss curves, making it difficult to select a 'best' model since rankings can change drastically across datasets.

There is sufficiently high variance in performance from random seed that performance improvements from random seed can exceed those from continuing to train on supervised fine-tuning data.

The instability in standard dense retrieval training stems from catastrophic forgetting phenomena, where models learn and forget different negative groups during training iterations that involve model training and hard negative selection.

Query sensitivity—the instability of retrieval results for semantically equivalent but lexically different queries—is a practical concern in dense retrieval.

Recent research also reveals that dense retrieval's interface is brittle for identity-level matching, as minimal compositional edits (negation, role swaps) that flip meaning can retain high similarity, and adding structure-targeted negatives consistently reduces zero-shot retrieval performance.

## Zobel 1998 Pooling Depth Analysis

Zobel examined the dependence of collection quality on pool depth by downsampling pools from early TREC collections and noted substantial degradation in collection quality for a depth of 10 but not for a depth of 50. Zobel demonstrated that these "approximately complete" judgments produced by pooling were sufficient to fairly compare retrieval runs, using the leave-out-uniques (LOU) test, and found that for the TREC-5 ad hoc collection, using unique relevant documents increased a run's 11 point average precision score by an average of 0.5%.

## Evaluation Bias and Unjudged Documents

The idea behind pooling is to find enough relevant documents such that when unjudged documents are assumed to be nonrelevant the resulting judgment set is sufficiently complete and unbiased. However, the judgments produced by traditional pooling when the pools are too small relative to the total document set size can be biased in that they favor relevant documents that contain topic title words, and this phenomenon is wholly dependent on the collection size.

Leave-Out-Uniques (LOU) tests are a way of analyzing the reusability of a collection, in which the relevant documents retrieved by only one participating team are removed from the qrels files and all runs are then evaluated using the reduced qrels. I found search results for the MultiContrievers paper. Here's what the research shows:

## Overview

The study analyzes what information is lost versus preserved in dense retrievers compared to the language models they are based on (e.g., BERT versus Contriever).

## Methodology

The researchers trained 25 MultiContrievers initialized from MultiBert checkpoints, and this is the first study that includes variability over a large number of retriever initializations. They used information theoretic probing, also known as minimum description length (MDL) probing, to measure the information in MultiContriever representations.

## Key Findings on Checkpoint Selection and Variance

MultiContrievers have a very wide range of performance on BEIR benchmarks, despite identical loss curves, and it is not easy to select a 'best' model, since the best and worst model is not consistent across datasets - the ranking of each model can change, sometimes drastically.

MultiContriever performance is surprisingly sensitive to both random initialization and to data shuffle. Additionally, there is sufficiently high variance that performance improvements from random seed can exceed those from continuing to train on supervised fine-tuning data.

The research was published in 2024 at the BlackboxNLP Workshop and provides important insights into the variability and checkpoint selection challenges in dense retrieval systems.
